analysis.one_liner: Forces drug-benefit middlemen in the federal employees' health plan to disclose pricing and pass rebates through.
analysis.headline: A House subcommittee approved the bill by voice vote in March 2010, but the full committee never voted on it and it died when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targeted pharmacy benefit managers — the companies insurers hire to run prescription drug coverage — inside the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, the plan covering millions of federal workers, retirees, and their families. It would have banned 'spread pricing' (charging the insurer more than the PBM pays the pharmacy), required PBMs to pass nearly all manufacturer rebates and fees back to the plan, capped dispensing fees, restricted the sale of enrollees' claims data, given enrollees an itemized explanation of benefits, and barred drug makers from owning the PBMs that negotiate their prices. The bill died in committee without a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 8 million federal employees, retirees, and family members enrolled in FEHBP would pay less for prescriptions and see itemized statements showing what each drug really cost and what the middleman and insurer pocketed. Taxpayers, who help fund the program, would share in the savings. Independent retail pharmacies would benefit from rules barring PBMs from steering prescriptions to mail-order arms they own and from reimbursing pharmacies less than they charge insurers.

how_it_helps.text: Bans spread pricing: a PBM cannot charge the health plan more for a drug than it pays the pharmacy that dispensed it, and must disclose its reimbursement formulas [S3].

Requires PBMs to pay the health plan at least 99 percent of all manufacturer payments they receive each quarter, including rebates, market-share incentives, and data-sale revenue, reported drug by drug [S3].
Gives enrollees the right to an explanation of benefits within 90 days of a fill, showing what the patient, the PBM, and the insurer each paid for the drug [S3].
Bars pharmaceutical manufacturers and retail pharmacies from controlling a PBM, and blocks a carrier from profiting off a PBM it owns, to limit conflicts of interest in drug negotiation [S3].
Requires manufacturers to report average manufacturer prices each quarter as a condition of getting paid under the program, and lets OPM and its inspector general examine PBM contracts [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers would lose the hidden spread, rebate retention, and data-sale revenue the bill targeted, and would bear new disclosure and audit obligations. Drug manufacturers would face quarterly price reporting and restrictions on the deals they strike with PBMs. Health plans administering FEHBP would carry new certification and compliance duties, some of which could show up in premiums.

drawbacks.text: The bill gives itself an exemption from the Freedom of Information Act for the pricing data OPM collects, so much of the new information would remain confidential and unavailable to the public [S3].
New disclosure, reporting, and audit requirements could raise administrative costs for PBMs and FEHBP plans, some portion of which could be passed into premiums.

Restrictions on drug substitutions and dispensing fees could limit some cost-control tools PBMs use, and OPM was given authority to waive the requirements for contract year 2011, softening the immediate effect [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real savings and honest pricing for federal drug coverage against higher compliance costs and less public access to the collected pricing data. The bill addressed documented practices — spread pricing and rebate retention — that shift drug costs onto enrollees and the government, so the benefits plausibly outweigh the administrative costs, but the FOIA exemption is a genuine design flaw that would keep the public from verifying the savings.

outcome.mechanism: A House subcommittee approved it in March 2010 by voice vote, but the full committee never scheduled a markup and the bill never reached the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Stephen Lynch introduced the bill on January 21, 2010, with Reps. Gerald Connolly and Elijah Cummings, and it was referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform [S5].
Sixteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S4].

It was referred to the Federal Workforce subcommittee, which held a hearing in February 2010, marked it up on March 24, 2010, and forwarded it to the full committee in amended form by voice vote [S5].
The full Oversight and Government Reform Committee took no further action, and no vote was ever recorded in the House or Senate before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug manufacturers kept the rebate, spread-pricing, and data-sale arrangements the bill would have restricted, and FEHBP enrollees kept paying whatever those arrangements produced. The sponsors and the subcommittee that approved the bill got nothing for their work.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug makers

sides.party_line_note: All 17 members who introduced or cosponsored the bill were House Democrats and no Republican signed on; no recorded votes were ever taken, so the full partisan shape was never measured.

industries.note: The bill bans spread pricing, forces nearly all rebates and manufacturer payments back to the plan, caps dispensing fees, restricts sales of claims data, and opens PBM contracts to government inspection — the practices that produce the industry's margin on federal drug coverage.

Manufacturers would have to report average manufacturer prices quarterly to keep getting paid under the program, and would be barred from controlling a PBM, limiting their ability to shape the middleman negotiating their prices.

PBMs could no longer require network participation as a condition of other networks, could not own a controlling interest in retail pharmacies, and could not pocket the spread between what they pay pharmacies and what they charge insurers, so pharmacy reimbursements would rise.

Carriers would receive at least 99 percent of PBM rebate and fee income, cutting their costs, but would take on annual certification and compliance duties and risk contract termination for PBM violations.
